When Ziyu asked for an article, Er Mu, about to leave for New York, refused at first. It had been ages since Er Mu had done any writing, and it was hard to think of anything good that would fit the theme of popular acoustics.

But when we met up again in Shanghai at the end of the month, Ziyu bought Er Mu off with a cheese-foam green tea from Heytea, the Chinese tea chain (regular cheese foam, less sugar, warm). And, of course, Er Mu had come across a little something in the Big Apple that seemed worth writing about.

New York, nicknamed the Big Apple, was first discovered by the Dutch, who founded New Amsterdam here. In the mid-seventeenth century the English took it over and renamed it New York in honor of the Duke of York.

As one of the world’s great cities, it has far too many places worth visiting: the Statue of Liberty, the Empire State Building, Central Park (Er Mu power-walked all the way around Central Park without finding the Central Park café), Broadway, Wall Street and more. Grand Central Terminal is one of them.

Like other famous sights, this classical Beaux-Arts building often appears in Hollywood films. Its most frequent screen roles go to the Main Concourse with its starry ceiling, and to the four-faced golden clock on the information booth in the middle of the hall.

The north side of the concourse leads to the platforms and the MetLife Building, and the south side has the ticket windows, which seem to look much as they did a hundred years ago. The timetable boards above the windows are now electronic, but they keep the look of the old mechanical ones. Er Mu first saw mechanical timetable boards in Europe and was fascinated by them. When the board updates, the flaps with the times on them flip over with a clatter, as if time itself were reminding everyone that it is slipping away. In this fully digital age, the mechanical boards still working in stations are like specimens left behind by the previous, electromechanical era: specimens you can see without going to a museum.

Walk out of the south side of the concourse and you reach another intriguing place, one that might even be enchanted: the Whispering Gallery.

It is really just an intersection where two underground passageways meet, under a curved, tiled Guastavino vault. With people streaming past, the background noise is so loud that two people a few meters apart can hardly make each other out even when they raise their voices. But if two people stand in diagonally opposite corners of the intersection, back to back and roughly 10 m apart, one can speak softly and the other hears clearly, as if they were standing right beside each other.

This counterintuitive long-distance transmission of sound is what makes the spot magical: in the middle of a noisy station, it gives two people a place to whisper. A private space inside the hubbub adds a touch of romance, and many New Yorkers have come here to declare their love.

This long-distance transmission of sound was first discovered in the circular gallery at the base of the dome of St. Paul’s Cathedral in London (one of the landmarks Churchill ordered protected at all costs during the Second World War). That is where the term “whispering gallery” comes from. Two people sitting at opposite ends of the gallery’s diameter, about 30 m apart, can talk to each other in whispers.

Back in the late nineteenth century, Lord Rayleigh (yes, the physicist who explained why the sky is blue) found that the sound travels along the curved wall, and that its intensity falls off in inverse proportion to the distance rather than with the inverse square, as in free space. That lets sound travel much farther. (Clap your hands once and you can hear about four echoes.)

So why does sound travel along the curved wall? It comes down to a family of special acoustic modes formed by the acoustically rigid, curved wall. The peaks of these modes are all concentrated in a ring-shaped region along the wall, as the figure below shows:

As the figure shows, these modes all have a high circumferential order, which also means high modal frequencies. In a whispering gallery, speaking softly works better and is easier to hear than speaking loudly. One reason is that the main frequency band of loud speech overlaps with the main band of the background noise, so the noise masks it strongly. The other is that soft speech has more high-frequency content, which excites these special modes more easily. Because these modes were first discovered in this special acoustic setting, they are called whispering-gallery modes.

It is worth mentioning that although they were first discovered in acoustics, whispering-gallery modes exist in many other fields too, such as optics and astrophysics: wherever there are waves, you will find them. They already have important practical applications, such as damage detection in materials and the development of new sensors.

The physics of whispering galleries means they turn up in many other places. One is the circular wall around the Imperial Vault of Heaven at the Temple of Heaven in Beijing, known as the Echo Wall, where two speakers can be 62 m apart. Another is the curved dam of the Barossa Reservoir, an hour’s drive north of Adelaide in Australia, where two people as far as 140 m apart can talk normally.

Can you hear me? Yep! Loud and clear!

These whispering galleries have one thing in common: they have all become well-known tourist attractions. While taking in the history, culture or natural scenery, visitors also get a small, delightful surprise from science.

Travel is romantic.

Knowing the history and culture behind a destination is romantic.

Understanding the science behind its curious physics can be romantic too.

Postscript

There is plenty to do in New York, and a Broadway show is an absolute must. The Phantom of the Opera and Chicago, each running for twenty or thirty years now, are popular choices for first-time visitors.

Phantom Chicago

Both shows have stood the test of time, and you won’t regret seeing either. But if you have to choose one, Er Mu would recommend the former from a sound point of view. Sound isn’t necessarily the most important thing in a musical, but good sound is definitely a plus: it helps bring the characters to life and draws the audience in. The immersive sound at the Majestic Theatre is sure to surprise you.

Last but not least, what self-respecting science article disguised as a travelogue would leave out photos and reviews of the latest Instagram-famous food?

So, so, so good!

Er Mu: Ziyu!

Ziyu: What?

Er Mu: Next time, can I order the Golden Phoenix Tea King?

Ziyu: You got it.

References:

1. C. V. Raman, “On the Whispering-Gallery Phenomenon,” 1921.

2. J. W. S. Rayleigh, Robert B. Lindsay, The Theory of Sound, 1945.

3. O. Wright, “Gallery of whispers,” 2012.

(Written to mark a late-night chance meeting at JFK with Yubo, a senior colleague: “Life is like a box of chocolates…”)
